papers.title: When Heating Enhances Dielectric Screening: Thermal Disordering of Surface-Templated Antiferroelectric Order Reverses the Temperature Response of Interfacial Water
papers.source: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abstract: Abstract The in-plane dielectric constant (ε∥) of nanoconfined water plays an essential role in temperature-gated nanofluidics and reaction kinetics at electrochemical interfaces. Water monolayers with antiferroelectric rhombic order on fcc(100) surfaces have been shown, in our previous work, to exhibit an anomalously low ε∥, but how this dielectric response evolves with temperature is unexplored. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we find that ε∥ of water on the fcc(100) surface increases monotonically with temperature, in stark contrast to the monotonic decrease observed on fcc(111) surfaces and in bulk water. This anomaly originates from the progressive thermal disordering of the antiferroelectric rhombic structure, releasing previously suppressed dipolar fluctuations. Consequently, the enhancement of the Kirkwood factor GK overcomes both the conventional 1/T thermal suppression and the concurrent loss of hydrogen bonds. By constructing a phase diagram of d(ln (ε∥ – 1))/d(ln T) in the temperature–surface interaction strength plane, we identify three distinct regimes governed by the surface–water interaction: monotonic increase, nonmonotonic behavior, and monotonic decrease. These findings establish a molecular mechanism for the dielectric temperature response of ordered water monolayers and provide a predictive framework for designing thermally programmable nanofluidic systems, with mechanistic insights relevant to electrochemical interfaces.

papers.abstract: The flow of molecularly confined water has attracted considerable interest in recent years. Yet despite their exquisite character, current nanofluidic devices cannot probe molecular water flow beyond the linear-response regime, while nanomechanical force- based approaches have produced markedly inconsistent results. Here, using tuning- fork-based atomic force microscopy, we tackle these limitations by measuring the full linear-to-nonlinear, shear-dependent viscoelastic rheology of molecularly confined water at various two-dimensional material interfaces -- demonstrating pronounced rate effects in water flow response. The observed rheological behaviors are remarkably analogous to that of macroscopic soft glassy yielding materials and fully captured by a non-linear model accounting for the shear-induced acceleration of the dynamics -- a hallmark of disordered supercooled and metastable systems. We further unveil a pronounced pressure-induced slowdown in nanoconfined water dynamics, with relaxation times extending into the microsecond range and marked material dependence. These results reveal non-linear, glassy rheology as a general feature of interfacial water and offer a route to tunable, non-linear nanofluidic elements.

papers.title: Selective Electronic Pre-Activation of OH Bonds in Extremely Confined Water
papers.abstract: Water under molecular-scale confinement is not simply a geometrically restricted form of bulk water, but can acquire distinct electronic, structural, and collective properties. However, how such an extremely confined state reshapes water's intrinsic chemistry remains poorly understood. Here, using ab initio calculations and enhanced-sampling machine-learning potential molecular dynamics, we show that extreme two-dimensional confinement activates water for proton generation. Monolayer-confined water exhibits a substantially lower free-energy barrier for forming separated H3O+ and OH- ions than bulk water, and this tendency is further enhanced by lateral compression and nuclear quantum fluctuations. This enhanced reactivity does not arise from a uniform weakening of all water molecules. Instead, confinement makes OH bonds breaking selectively. The water molecule contains electronically distinct OH bonds, with weak in-plane bonds preferentially activated for proton release, while stronger dangling bonds remain relatively inactive. The surrounding hydrogen-bond network then provides disordered pathways for proton relocation, and the enhanced in-plane polarization stabilizes the charged products. Our results suggest that two-dimensional confined water can act as an active and superdielectric medium as indicated by recent experiments. Our findings reveal extreme confinement as a route to tune water-mediated chemistry, with implications for nanofluidics, geochemical pores, biological environments, and catalytic interfaces.

papers.title: Balance between Geometric Confinement and Hydrogen Bond Strength Controls Water Dynamics in 2D hBN Nanopores
papers.source: The Journal of Physical Chemistry C
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigated the structural and dynamical properties of water confined within hexagonal boron nitride nanopores using molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning potentials trained on ab initio data. Density profiles reveal pronounced layering behavior, with a distinct bilayer structure observed within the 9-Å pore size. Diffusion coefficients exhibit non-monotonic dependence on pore size, with water confined in 10-Å pores exhibiting the highest value among the other pores considered. Water confined within the 9-Å pore shows the lowest diffusivity despite having the weakest hydrogen-bond network. This demonstrates that geometric confinement, rather than hydrogen bond strength, dominates water dynamics within the confined systems studied here. These findings demonstrate size-dependent confinement effects with a transition regime at approximately 10 Å, where relaxation of spatial constraints considerably enhances water mobility. Infrared spectra reveal confinement and interface-induced shifts and broadening of vibrational features, reflecting altered hydrogen-bond environments and dynamical heterogeneity across pore sizes. The use of machine-learned potentials enables an accurate description of polarization, hydrogen-bond fluctuations, and vibrational dynamics under confinement, which are not fully captured by conventional force fields. These combined results demonstrate a confinement-driven crossover governed by the interplay between geometry, interfacial chemistry, and hydrogen-bonding dynamics, providing key insight for predicting and tuning transport in nanofluidic and interfacial systems. Consistent with prior observations, layering appears to be primarily controlled by confinement geometry, while surface chemistry influences molecular orientation and interfacial ordering.

papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding the behavior of water confined in atomic-scale channels is a cornerstone of nanoscience and nanofluidics. Unlike graphene, isostructural hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spontaneously acquires electric charges in liquid water due to hydroxide ion (OH–) adsorption. Yet, whether this reactivity persists under monolayer and bilayer confinement remains an open question. Here, we use first-principles modeling to uncover the role of stacking symmetry (AA vs AA’) between hBN walls─a factor that has so far received little attention in boron nitride systems─on the structural and dynamical properties of Å-scale water. We systematically probe neutral, alkaline, and acidic environments to elucidate how water self-ions (H3O+ and OH–) interact with hBN interfaces. Combining ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations with machine learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) for extended time scales, we obtain a consistent description, at the revPBE-D3 level of theory, of water’s structural and transport properties under extreme confinement. Our results demonstrate that stacking symmetry critically impacts monolayer water systems and modulates the energetics of chemisorbed hydroxide and interfacial friction. In alkaline conditions, chemisorbed hydroxide doubles friction, yet its effect on water diffusion is minimal. Strikingly, monolayer water exhibits a twofold diffusion enhancement compared to bilayer water, reaching bulk-like values─revealing that diffusion is an intrinsic property of the water layer, independent of wall chemistry. This work delivers quantitative estimates of friction and diffusion coefficients, conditional on the chosen functional and water loadings, that provide a reference for future experiments on Å-scale water transport.

papers.abstract: Hydration layers are widely recognized as the molecular basis of antifouling membrane interfaces, yet their role is still largely viewed through a static barrier picture. The dynamic response of hydrated membrane-water interfaces to approaching foulants, particularly under organic-inorganic mixed fouling conditions, remains poorly understood. Here, using poly(sulfobetaine methacrylate) (pSBMA)-modified nanofiltration membranes as a model zwitterionic interface, we reveal that fouling reversibility is strongly influenced by the dynamic stability of hydrogen-bonded hydration networks at the membrane-water interface. Molecular simulations combined with sum-frequency generation spectroscopy demonstrate that pSBMA sustains a strongly hydrogen-bonded interfacial water structure with preferential water dipole orientation under silicate and alginate perturbation, thereby suppressing long-lived foulant residence near the membrane surface. Real-time surface plasmon resonance measurements further confirm weakened irreversible foulant anchoring and enhanced interfacial reversibility. As a result, pSBMA-modified nanofiltration membranes reduced flux decline during mixed-foulant filtration to ∼6% and achieved >91% flux recovery after physical cleaning, accompanied by lower organic and inorganic foulant residuals. Repeated filtration-cleaning tests with real secondary effluent further confirmed nearly complete flux recovery in complex water matrices. These findings revisit zwitterionic antifouling by shifting the focus from static surface hydration to the dynamic stability of hydrogen-bonded hydration networks, providing a mechanistic basis for understanding and regulating fouling reversibility.

papers.abstract: Directional proton transport is central to bioenergetics and emerging electrochemical technologies, yet achieving high and anisotropic proton conductivity in fully covalent, charge-neutral crystalline materials remains a challenge. Here, we report anisotropic proton conduction in a one-dimensional covalent polymer single crystal mediated by confined water wires. A phenylalanine-tyrosine-based monomer bearing azide and alkyne termini undergoes topochemical click reaction via large-amplitude molecular rotations, yielding a 1,4-triazole-linked one-dimensional polymer through a single-crystal-to-single-crystal transformation. The polymerization concomitantly generates hydrophobic nanochannels that reversibly capture atmospheric water, within which water molecules self-assemble into extended hydrogen-bonded chains. Proton conductivity measured on individual crystals is significantly higher along the channels than perpendicular to them, revealing an intrinsic anisotropic transport. Notably, this fully organic polymer crystal, capable of harvesting atmospheric water, represents the highest-performing proton-conducting organic crystalline material without external charged species or proton carriers, establishing a blueprint for designing bioinspired peptide-based neutral systems with directional proton transport.

papers.abstract: Abstract Ion and water transport through subnanometer carbon nanotubes (CNTs) exhibits numerous anomalies absent in bulk solutions, yet the interplay among the confined water structure, external electric fields, and ion transport remains poorly understood. Here, we use systematic nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to study single-file water confined in a CNT of radius 0.37 nm, both in the absence and presence of a single Na+ ion, under applied electric fields ranging from 0 to 0.2 V Å–1. In the Na+–water–CNT system, the electroosmotic flow (EOF) velocity increases nonlinearly with the field. Such nonlinear enhancement is attributed to water ordering that is exclusive to the ion-containing system. This enhanced ordering is evidenced by a larger average number of hydrogen bonds per water molecule, longer hydrogen-bond lifetimes, a reduced interoxygen distance with a higher first peak in the oxygen–oxygen radial distribution function, and a decrease in free energy. Further relative permittivity calculations reveal that the effective permittivity decreases with increasing electric field, leading to a monotonic rise in the Born energy difference between the Na+–water–CNT and water–CNT systems. This increase in Born energy likely drives the observed water ordering in Na+–water–CNT. Our findings uncover a previously unrecognized coupling mechanism among ions, electric fields, and water structure under extreme confinement.

papers.title: Asymmetric In-Plane Dielectric Response of Interfacial Water to Biaxial Strain: Decoupling Orientational and Positional Order
papers.abstract: Abstract Antiferroelectric (AFE) ordering in interfacial water strongly suppresses its in-plane dielectric constant, yet how to actively tune the dielectric response of AFE ordered water remains largely unexplored. Here, using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on a model platinum surface, we investigate the influence of mechanical strain on the dielectric behavior of ordered interfacial water. The in-plane dielectric constant ε∥ exhibits an asymmetric V-shaped response to biaxial strain, where compression drives a sharp increase in ε∥ (∼2.52-fold), while tension induces a modest rise (∼1.62-fold). This asymmetry originates from the fact that the regular oxygen sublattice is preserved under tension, which continues to constrain dipole orientations. As a result, the AFE order parameter η decreases by only ∼11%. By contrast, the ordered structure is severely disrupted under compression, with η dropping by ∼49%. Tension thus selectively decouples orientational order from positional order in AFE interfacial water, which limits the release of dipolar fluctuations, leading to a moderate rise in the Kirkwood correlation factor GK and, consequently, a gentle enhancement of ε∥. Our findings identify mechanical strain as an effective physical tool for selectively decoupling orientational and positional order at interface.

papers.abstract: Water confined to low dimensions exhibits even more anomalous behavior than bulk water. Since these anomalies are primarily dictated by hydrogen bonds (hbs), we investigate hb behavior in quasi-one-dimensional water chains using density functional theory. Furthermore, we show that repulsive interactions emerge when hbs become multifurcated. These additional repulsive forces weaken the hbs and play a crucial role in driving the structural transition. We demonstrate that the many-body interactions associated with hb cooperativity, as well as the repulsive forces from multifurcated hbs, are captured by classical dipole-dipole interactions. This indicates that both hb cooperativity and the weakening of multifurcated hbs are classical electrostatic phenomena, even though quantum effects dictate the strength of the effective dipoles involved. Finally, we discuss how these results provide insights for understanding the flow mechanism of water along pores of sub-nanometer diameter and aid in developing a simple, universal water model.

papers.abstract: Water in soft electrochemical materials is far more than a passive solvent-it directly governs ionic transport, dielectric response, and structural stability. papers.abstract: Dielectric screening of electric fields is modified by interfaces and confinement, and any accurate description of interfacial chemistry necessitates properly modeling the nonuniform dielectric tensor. However, models with short range interactions, such as local machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), are increasingly used in simulations of molecular interfaces without quantitative understanding of their nonuniform dielectric response. To build this understanding, we use the framework provided by local molecular field (LMF) theory to quantify the roles of short and long range electrostatics in confined water. Short and long range models predict the same transverse dielectric profile but short range models predict qualitatively different longitudinal dielectric profiles than their long range counterparts. To understand these differences, we develop a Landau theory that shows that long range interactions stiffen polarization fluctuations by a factor of the bulk dielectric constant and reduce the interfacial polarization correlation length by an order of magnitude. LMF theory, which captures long range interactions with an averaged field, can correct the structure and dielectric response, but the standard fluctuation relation no longer holds. We derive a fluctuation relation and integral equation for LMF theory and demonstrate their accuracy for predicting longitudinal dielectric response. MLIPs that incorporate interfacial configurations in their training essentially learn a static mean field correction at the interface, such that the integral equation can be used to predict their nonuniform dielectric profile from polarization fluctuations. We also show that short range MLIPs can be combined with symmetry preserving mean field (SPMF) theory to provide a linear-scaling alternative for long range interactions and predicting nonuniform dielectric functions.

papers.abstract: Modern instruments used to observe water at interfaces can distinguish individual molecular layers, measure dielectric permittivity within nanometer-scale gaps, and track reorientation on femtosecond timescales. We attribute this disconnect to three factors: the term “structure” refers to three independent properties of water; the parameters typically controlled are not actually independent variables; and the state of water influences material performance through multiple pathways that yield opposing effects. papers.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) synthesis, yet its efficiency is limited by sluggish N–O bond cleavage, incomplete NOx hydrogenation, and competing hydrogen evolution reaction. However, how catalyst structural engineering regulates the interfacial microenvironment remains unclear, despite its critical importance for constructing efficient catalysts. Here, we report a Cu3Ru7 catalyst with abundant Cu–Ru interfaces, where interface-induced water reorganization enables efficient NH3 production. The Cu3Ru7 catalyst exhibits an impressive NH3 formation rate of 19.7 mmol h–1 cm–2 at 5 A cm–2 in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer and remains stable at 2 A cm–2 with an NH3 Faradaic efficiency of ∼86% for 500 h. A scale-up demonstration using a 100 cm2 MEA electrolyzer affords an NH3 formation rate up to 1.5 mol h–1 at 400 A. The in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) reveals that Cu3Ru7 catalyst establishes a moderate interfacial hydrogen-bond network, which creates a water-mediated interfacial micro environment that facilitates NOx deoxygenation and subsequent NHx formation. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations further reveal that the Cu–Ru interface stabilizes the dissociating oxygen atom through a persistent and dynamically connected hydrogen-bond network, thereby facilitating sequential NO3– → NO2 → NO conversion. Meanwhile, the surrounding Cu matrix attenuates the excessive *H accumulation characteristic of Ru, suppressing the hydrogen evolution reaction. This work establishes Cu–Ru interface-induced interfacial water reorganization as a strategy for improving electrocatalytic nitrate reduction performance.

papers.title: Microscopic Origins of Metal‐Dependent pH Effects in Hydrogen Evolution: Metal–Water Interactions Dictate Proton Transfer Pathways
papers.abstract: The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a prototypical proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) reaction, yet the atomistic origin of its metal-dependent pH effect remains unclear. Here, combining constant-potential ab initio molecular dynamics with in situ infrared spectroscopy, we unravel the microscopic origins of metal-dependent pH effects in HER catalysis on Pt(111) and Au(111). We reveal that HER kinetics are governed by two competing spatial proton transfer topologies associated with the Volmer water-dissociation step: a low-barrier cross-layer proton transfer (CLPT) pathway and a high-barrier intra-layer proton transfer (ILPT) pathway. For Pt(111), strong metal-water interactions yield a pH-responsive water network. Under acidic conditions, a balanced intra- and cross-layer hydrogen-bond network promotes the CLPT in the Volmer step, thereby accelerating HER kinetics. By contrast, alkaline media induce a rigid H-down interfacial water layer that favors the sluggish ILPT pathway. Conversely, weak metal-water interactions on Au(111) maintain a pH-insensitive, predominantly parallel-flat water orientation that restricts the Volmer step to cooperate only with the high-barrier ILPT in both acidic and alkaline solutions. Our findings establish a fundamental causal link among metal-water interactions, interfacial hydrogen-bonding network, proton transfer pathways, and HER kinetics, providing atomistic insight into the design of pH-robust electrocatalysts.

papers.title: Molecular Insights into the Growth/Dissociation of CH4 Hydrate under the Calcite Slit-Pore Confinement: Effect of Pore Size Variation
papers.abstract: In nature, CH4 hydrates occur within marine sediments characterized by varying pore size, geometry, and composition, all of which influence hydrate phase transition. Although molecular dynamics (MD) studies of confined hydrates often focus on silicate pores, hydrate reservoirs also contain carbonates, which may exhibit hydrate behaviour distinct from silicates. Hence, in this MD study, we investigate the effect of calcite slit-pore size variation on the dissociation temperature (T3) of CH4 hydrate, as well as the dynamics of confined water and methane molecules within calcite pores. To this end, we perform direct phase co-existence MD simulations of CH4 hydrate confined in calcite slit-pores of three different pore sizes (i.e., ∼3.8, ∼6.2, and ∼8.6 nm), in the NVT ensemble at 270, 280, 290, and 300 K. Our results indicate that decreasing slit-pore size shifts the T3 range for CH4 hydrate to lower temperatures, with the smallest pore exhibiting the fastest dissociation. The mechanisms of hydrate cage distortion near the hydrate-calcite surface interface and the formation of the bound interfacial water layer have been elucidated for the small slit-pore system, along with hydrogen bond analysis to explain the microscopic origins of our simulation observations. In contrast to the hydrophilic silica slit-pores studied previously (Fluid Phase Equilibria 2025, 588, 114218), the CH4 cluster confined in the calcite slit-pore tends to remain away from the calcite surface. This behavior arises from the strong electrostatic interaction between the calcite surface and water molecules, which creates a layer of ordered bound water. The potential of the mean force calculation reveals that this bound water layer imposes a higher energy barrier for the CH4 molecule near the calcite surface. The relative location of the CH4 hydrate with respect to the CH4 cluster and/or the calcite substrate influences the hydrate growth and dissociation mechanism.

papers.title: Revealing Sequential Stages of Excited-State Water Chemistry on a Monolayer Covalent Triazine Framework
papers.abstract: Abstract Direct spectroscopic identification of the earliest stages of interfacial water activation remains a major challenge in photocatalysis, as the first reaction intermediates are short-lived and rapidly evolve into more stable products. Here, we investigate water activation on an electronically excited two-dimensional covalent triazine framework (CTF) grown on Au(111) using localized water dosing and synchrotron X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Room-temperature measurements reveal persistent chemical species consistent with products of the reaction at the water/CTF interface, whereas low-temperature experiments under an ice overlayer reveal a spectroscopic signature assigned to protonation of triazine nitrogen. This transient feature, likely stabilized by the ice environment, may represent the earliest experimentally accessible chemical consequence of the excited-state water−CTF interaction. Its spectroscopic fingerprint is consistent with the initial proton-transfer step proposed in excited-state proton-coupled electron-transfer (ES-PCET) descriptions of water activation. These results provide direct spectroscopic access to transient interfacial species involved in the initial phase of photocatalytic water activation and establish experimental constraints for mechanistic descriptions based on PCET.

papers.title: Adhesion and moisture-induced debonding mechanisms at asphalt–recycled concrete aggregate interfaces: molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry insights
papers.abstract: Recycled concrete aggregate (RCA) offers a sustainable way to reuse waste concrete in asphalt pavements, but weak bonding between asphalt and adhered cement mortar increases moisture susceptibility. This study investigated the mineral-specific adhesion and moisture-induced debonding mechanisms at asphalt–RCA interfaces. Molecular dynamics simulations and quantum chemistry calculations were combined to examine wetting, adhesion and dynamic separation on calcium silicate hydrate (CSH), ettringite (AFt), monosulfate (AFm) and SiO₂ surfaces. Mean contact angles ranged from 118.3° to 137.4° for asphalt and from 16.8° to 39.0° for water. Dry adhesion energy followed AFt > CSH > SiO₂ > AFm and was dominated by van der Waals interactions. Interfacial water displaced asphalt fractions and reduced adhesion. With a 4 Å water layer, adhesion energies decreased to 29.6–34.7 mJ/m²; AFm retained 37.4% of its dry adhesion energy, whereas AFt retained 20.7%. Water also reduced the adhesion-energy change during dynamic separation. Resins and aromatics were the major contributors to adhesion energies, while quantum chemical descriptors identified potential interaction sites. These findings link mineral surface chemistry and water redistribution to asphalt adhesion and debonding, providing molecular-level insight for RCA pretreatment and moisture-durability improvement.

papers.abstract: Abstract The tumor suppressor protein p53 is a sequence-specific transcription factor whose DNA-binding domain (DBD) is essential for maintaining genomic stability. Mutations at residues that directly contact DNA frequently impair DNA recognition and are strongly associated with tumorigenesis. In this study, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the impact of frequent contact mutations (R248Q, R248W, R273C, and R273H) on the dynamics, energetics, and hydration properties of the p53-DNA complex. Comparative analysis of wild-type (WT) and mutant complexes reveals that these mutations perturb hydrogen-bonding and electrostatic interaction networks and alter the solvation environment at the DNA-binding interface, leading to less favorable binding free energies, as quantified by alchemical free energy calculations. Analysis of interfacial water dynamics shows that water molecules in the WT complex are more ordered and long-lived, forming stable water bridges that reinforce protein–DNA contacts. The mutations are accompanied by changes in the interfacial hydration network, including mutation-dependent variations in water-bridge occupancy, water mobility, rotational dynamics, and H-bond relaxation lifetimes. These molecular changes are associated with altered solvation contributions and reduced binding affinity in the mutant systems.

papers.abstract: Accurately predicting the steep, S-shaped water adsorption isotherms of mildly hydrophobic MOFs and other hydrophobic porous materials remains challenging. This difficulty stems from the delicate balance between framework–water and water–water interactions that governs cooperative pore filling. Here, we develop a machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP), trained on reliable density functional theory reference data, for the prototypical mildly hydrophobic channel MOF MIP-211(Al). Combined with a Molecular Dynamics-based transition-matrix Monte Carlo (MD-TMMC) scheme, this accurate MLIP enables to predict the sorption isotherm in excellent agreement with the corresponding experimental data, capturing both the low-pressure gradual water uptake increase and the sharp adsorption step at P/P0 ≈ 0.3. This accuracy enables to elucidate the adsorption mechanism, from initial adsorption to complete pore filling: water first anchors through a characteristic OCOO···H2O···μ-OH dual hydrogenbond interaction motif; as these sites saturate, a secondary and competitive OCOO···H2O···H2O dual interaction motif emerges, driving cooperative self-assembly and triggering the adsorption step. At saturation, the confined water network approaches, but does not fully reach, bulk-water connectivity. This work demonstrates that combining a reliable MLIP-training level of theory with an appropriate MC strategy enables both quantitative prediction and mechanistic understanding of water adsorption, providing a foundation for the rational design of mildly hydrophobic MOFs of key interest for heat transformation technologies and water harvesting applications.

papers.abstract: Abstract Water scarcity and land desertification are interconnected global challenges requiring materials that simultaneously enable freshwater production and sand stabilization. Herein, we develop a gelation-directed hierarchical particle-reinforced (HPR) organohydrogel by integrating polydopamine (PDA)-decorated sand particles into a poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA) network. The PDA layer provides broadband photothermal conversion while strengthening the sand-PVA interface, facilitating interfacial stress transfer, whereas the sand particles reinforce the polymer network and stabilize the granular framework. Meanwhile, the hydrated PVA network regulates confined water and lowers its evaporation enthalpy by 20.6–24.3%, while the hierarchical architecture preserves interconnected pathways for water and ion transport. The optimized HPR organohydrogel achieves an evaporation rate of 2.12 kg m–2 h–1 and an apparent efficiency of 94.3% under one-sun irradiation, with stable performance under repeated cycling, high salinity, extreme acidic/alkaline, and oil-contaminated conditions. Notably, evaporation-induced salt enrichment triggers Hofmeister interactions that further strengthen the hydrogel-sand framework, establishing positive feedback between solar evaporation and sand stabilization. This gelation-directed interfacial reinforcement strategy transforms hydrogel formation into a functional assembly process, exploring the potential for coupling solar-driven freshwater generation with ecological sand stabilization.

papers.title: Self-driven beta-radiation detection through a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure
papers.abstract: Large-volume neutrino observatories, exemplified by IceCube, exploit Cherenkov light generated by neutrino-induced charged particles in Antarctic ice, highlighting the potential of water-based media for high-energy particle detection. In $β$-decay, a neutron converts into a proton via the weak interaction, emitting an electron and an electron antineutrino. The electron constitutes the beta radiation detected in this work, while the accompanying antineutrino motivates future extensions toward neutrino detection. Here we demonstrate a complementary electrical transduction strategy using a graphene/water/silicon heterostructure that generates reversible current transients under beta irradiation at zero applied bias. Energetic electrons deposit energy in silicon, producing nonequilibrium carriers that perturb the semiconductor surface potential and electric displacement across the adjacent aqueous interface. The resulting redistribution of interfacial water polarization drives a transient compensation current, whereas carrier relaxation restores the initial polarization state and generates an opposite-polarity recovery signal. The complete irradiation-detector-electrometer system exhibits exponential rise and recovery time constants of approximately 1.0 and 3.6 ms, respectively. The response is strongly regulated by water-layer thickness and ionic composition, and the 17 beam pulses of a programmed 1 s sequence at 17 Hz are resolved individually. Integration with Ce:YAG further introduces a scintillation-mediated excitation pathway. These findings establish interfacial water polarization as a tunable, zero-bias electrical transduction mechanism for time-resolved beta-radiation monitoring and motivate future investigations of higher-energy charged particles and secondary particles relevant to neutrino detection.

papers.abstract: Abstract Understanding electrochemical reaction mechanisms requires atomistic simulations that simultaneously capture charged interfaces, explicit solvent, and long-time dynamics, which remain beyond the reach of conventional ab initio molecular dynamics. papers.title: Adsorption of cations at electrochemical interfaces revisited
papers.abstract: At electrochemical interfaces, alkali-metal and alkaline-earth metal cations are usually described as solvated species that nonspecifically adsorb, whereas specifically adsorbed anions interact more directly with metal electrodes. However, the mode of cation-surface interaction remains poorly defined at the atomic scale because experiments typically measure averaged interfacial responses. Distinguishing hydration modulated polarization from localized ion-surface coupling therefore requires access to both the atomic structure and the redistribution of electronic charge. Using density functional theory molecular dynamics, we reexamine this distinction for hydrated K+, Na+, Ca2+, oand Mg2+ at Pt(111), Au(111), and Ag(111) metal-water interfaces. Charge neutral, symmetric 3 × 3 cells containing one cation and five to seven water molecules at each interface allow for the study of compact, ion-rich layer configurations, rather than dilute electrolytes or electrodes maintained at an applied potential. Within the sampled compact layer configurations, structural sampling and charge density difference analysis indicate that cation adsorption spans a continuum of interfacial responses, ranging from diffuse, hydration modulated polarization to localized, compact layer coupling. Divalent cations exhibit the most persistent direct contact, and the selected divalent configurations show localized electronic redistribution, while monovalent cations are more sensitive to water coverage and substrate identity. Even predominantly non-contact cations can remain electronically relevant by polarizing the interfacial water layer and metal surface. These results suggest that cation adsorption within the compact interfacial region requires a local, structure dependent description that goes beyond simple specific or nonspecific classifications.

papers.abstract: Abstract While product-induced inhibition is widely recognized in heterogeneous catalysis, the joint influence of co-generated products on time-dependent catalytic deactivation remains underexplored. Herein, uniform colloidal Pt nanoparticles were deposited on anatase TiO2 supports selectively exposing (101) or (001) facets to fabricate two facet-controlled model Pt/TiO2 catalysts. We uncovered the intrinsic deactivation mechanism for low-temperature lean propylene combustion via stability tests, alternating feed kinetics, in situ DRIFTS, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Time-on-stream reaction tests recorded persistent activity decay for both catalysts, with far more serious decay observed on Pt/TiO2(101). Multiple characterization results excluded Pt sintering/encapsulation, C3H6/O2 poisoning, and partial Pt oxidation as dominant degradation factors. Instead, CO2 adsorption and subsequent carbonate accumulation on TiO2 surfaces were identified as the primary deactivation sources, which cut off supplementary oxygen delivery at metal–support interfaces. DFT adsorption energy data proved that H2O possessed a stronger surface affinity than CO2 on both facet types, and in situ generated H2O competed for adsorption sites to curb carbonate accumulation. Apart from this competitive effect, reaction-derived H2O alleviated excessive coverage of Pt sites by C3H6 and facilitated the adsorption and activation of gas-phase O2. Thanks to the relatively high water-binding capacity of TiO2(001), the corresponding Pt/TiO2(001) catalyst maintained abundant interfacial water during operation and exhibited much milder carbonate-triggered decay. These findings clarified the competitive co-adsorption interplay between CO2 and H2O across Pt–TiO2 interfaces and offered general kinetic guidance for developing durable catalysts toward industrial hydrocarbon lean combustion.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Efficient regulation of the hydrogen and hydroxyl binding energies (HBE/OHBE) lies at the core of developing high‐performance alkaline hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) electrocatalysts, yet it remains challenging due to the inherent correlation between the two binding energies. Herein, we demonstrate a d ‐electron modulation strategy on dual‐metal sites to break the scaling constraint and synergistically optimize HBE and OHBE. A well‐defined Cu‐based two‐dimensional conductive metal–organic framework (Cu‐HHTP) serves as a universal host to incorporate various 3 d transition metals (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu), yielding M–Cu dual sites with finely tunable d ‐electron configurations. Density functional theory calculations combined with experiments reveal that higher d ‐electron occupancy of the secondary metal site lowers the d ‐band center, and the water dissociation energy barrier exhibits a typical volcano‐type trend. The Co–Cu dual sites at the volcano apex promote the Volmer step through optimized OHBE and water adsorption. Meanwhile, this dual‐site configuration promotes the rearrangement of interfacial water molecules by disrupting the hydrogen‐bond network, thereby optimizing HBE. This work decouples HBE and OHBE via d ‐electron configuration, shifting the design paradigm from empirical screening to predictive design.

papers.title: Phase engineering of Mo x C regulates electronic structure and interfacial hydrogen-bond networks over Ru sites for pH-universal hydrogen evolution
papers.abstract: Abstract Metallic ruthenium (Ru) represents a promising Pt alternative for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). However, achieving efficient HER, particularly under pH-universal conditions, remains challenging due to sluggish interfacial water dissociation kinetics. Herein, we report a phase engineering strategy that utilizes well-defined cubic and hexagonal molybdenum carbide (α–MoC/β–Mo2C) supports to regulate Ru–MoxC metal–support interactions and interfacial microenvironments. The Ru–MoC exhibits superior performance to Ru–Mo2C across a wide pH range. Notably, the Ru–MoC requires an overpotential of 12 mV at 10 mA cm−2 in alkaline media, outperforming most previously reported catalysts. Moreover, no activity loss occurs during 80 h of reaction, demonstrating the good durability of the Ru–MoC. Detailed characterizations reveal that the electron-rich Ru centers in Ru–MoC induce stronger interfacial polarization. The enhanced polarization enables effective reorganization of interfacial hydrogen-bond networks into a beneficial dynamic and weakly hydrogen-bonded state for water dissociation in alkaline medium. This work provides new insights into the regulation of interfacial catalytic microenvironments, offering a promising strategy for the design of advanced nanocatalysts.

PUMA@Zn//I 2 cells retain 88% capacity after 43 000 cycles at 4 A g −1 and operate for over 11 000 cycles even at high iodine loading (16.58 mg cm −2 ). This strategy provides a novel pathway to achieve robust, ion‐conductivity, and chemically bonded hydrogel–metal interfaces for high‐performance aqueous batteries.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) are central to renewable‐powered green hydrogen production. As the benchmark electrocatalyst for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), conventional single‐phase IrO 2 is constrained by linear scaling relations among oxygenated intermediates, compounded by severe mass‐transport limitations and poorly regulated interfacial water structures. Here, we design a Turing‐type MoO x ‐IrO 2 heterostructure with strongly coupled cluster‐scale interfaces, which enables dual‐function Ir‐Mo synergy that breaks fundamental kinetic limitations and optimizes interfacial water structures. At the reaction pathway level, Brønsted‐acidic MoO x clusters promote water dissociation to generate reactive Mo─OH* intermediates, triggering radical coupling with adjacent Ir─O* species to form OOH* and thus circumventing the linear scaling relation. At the interfacial microenvironment level, MoO x reorganizes the rigid hydrogen‐bonding networks and increases the population of free H 2 O species, effectively alleviating concentration overpotentials under high‐current‐density operation. When integrated into a practical 25 cm 2 membrane electrode assembly, this catalyst delivers a PEMWE cell voltage of 1.71 V at 3 A cm −2 and an ultralow degradation rate of ∼9.5 µV h −1 over 1000 h, with a total platinum‐group‐metal loading of merely 0.5 mg cm −2 across both electrodes. Our dual‐modulation strategy establishes a transformative paradigm for developing low‐iridium and durable OER electrocatalysts toward practical green hydrogen production.

papers.title: Lipid Headgroup Hydration Regulates Distinct Remodeling of the Membrane Interface by Polyethylene Glycol and Dextran
papers.abstract: Water-soluble polymers commonly interact with cell membranes, but their interactions are poorly understood. Here, we investigate polyethylene glycol (PEG) and dextran (DEX) interactions with different model lipid membranes. Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we observe that PEG and DEX trigger strikingly different membrane responses - DEX induces extensive membrane remodeling, including localized multilamellar domain formation, while PEG does not. Combining fluorescence spectroscopy, fluorescence anisotropy, and vibrational sum frequency spectroscopy, we show that DEX perturbs lipid headgroup hydration by displacing interfacial water with minimal effects on lipid packing, while PEG largely preserves this hydration layer. We find that membrane binding affinity alone does not determine the extent to which hydrophilic polymers perturb membrane structure and interfacial properties; and that lipid headgroup hydration, rather than lipid charge, is a general regulator of hydrophilic polymer-membrane interactions. This work gives mechanistic insights into how neutral polymers interact with cells and vesicles, with relevance to cell biology and drug delivery.

papers.title: Ion-Specific Interfacial Hydration Beyond Classical Chaotropicity
papers.source: The Journal of Physical Chemistry B
papers.abstract: Ion specificity at charged aqueous interfaces plays important roles in many natural and technological phenomena. While ion-specific effects have been frequently investigated for halides and other molecular anions, the bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI) anion, a common ionic liquid anion, has been rarely investigated in aqueous interfaces. However, TFSI-water interactions are highly important in rare earth element separations. Here, using sum-frequency generation (SFG) spectroscopy, we demonstrate that TFSI restructures water at a positively charged imidazolium Langmuir monolayer interface through a mechanism qualitatively different from those of the conventional chaotropes thiocyanate and nitrate. Specifically, we study TFSI-, SCN-, and NO3- adsorption at a 1-octadecyl-3-methylimidazolium (C18mim) Langmuir monolayer over a 250 nM to 10 mM concentration range. Direct SO2 and CN vibrational signatures quantified TFSI and SCN adsorption, respectively. The OH stretch response was used to characterize ion-induced changes in the interfacial water structure and diffuse-layer screening. TFSI- adsorbs exceptionally strongly with an apparent adsorption free energy of -36.8 kJ/mol. Its OH band response is fundamentally different from that of SCN- and NO3-. After TFSI- SO2 stretch signal saturates, the hydrogen-bonded OH signal continues to decrease and a distinct high frequency band at ∼3620 cm-1 persists. These results identify an asymmetric hydration shell of TFSI as an additional structural factor in ion specificity.

papers.source: Journal of the American Chemical Society

papers.abstract: In living cells, the conversion of squalene to lanosterol requires two dedicated enzymes and proceeds through 2,3-oxidosqualene as an essential intermediate. We show that water microdroplets contacting immiscible organic solvents accomplish this same multistep transformation without enzymatic catalysis. We propose that the oriented electric field across the water-organic interface generates reactive oxygen species that epoxidize squalene and then initiates acid-catalyzed ring-opening of the epoxide followed by a cationic polyene cyclization cascade to yield lanosterol. H218O labeling traced oxygen from water into TEMPO-derived and peroxyacetate ions observed by real-time mass spectrometry. LC-HRMS/MS further revealed C18-C30 reaction products with spectral matches to oxygenated terpenoid and steroid-like structures. We find that ethyl acetate is the most effective organic solvent because it generates peroxyacetic acid at the interface. Simulations show that a preformed protonated 2,3-oxidosqualene model remains hydrated and oriented after placement at the ethyl acetate-water interface, and calculations on microsolvation models indicate that an interfacial water configuration preferentially stabilizes the epoxidation transition state relative to the reactant by approximately 3 kcal mol-1. These results establish a plausible, abiotic pathway for steroid emergence and diversification at water-organic interfaces.

papers.abstract: A water droplet moving over a solid substrate undergoes repeated renewal of its contact region while exchanging matter, charge, and interfacial forces with the surface. Co-author Ivan Stefanov reported observing a pronounced, rapid change in the apparent mechanical consistency of an initially pure water droplet rolling over freshly ground and cleaned microscope glass, described as honey-like thickening. The physical character of this response is examined using published measurements of silica–water hydration, glass dissolution and colloidal transfer, internal circulation of moving drops, and rheological changes in confined or particle-bearing aqueous systems. We analyze glass and water as interacting compartments whose states can evolve during contact. Material gain and loss, rolling-dependent exposure, and the distinction between bulk viscosity and interfacial resistance provide a quantitative basis for interpreting the observed response. Two sequential-transfer pathways are considered: subsequent water contacting the previously exposed glass and water contacting a second vessel previously exposed to the treated droplet. Matched chemical, rheological, surface and flow measurements are specified to distinguish these pathways and identify the physical carriers. Together, these observations and relationships define an experimentally accessible problem of formation, persistence and transfer of aqua structure at water–solid interfaces.

topics.name: Adsorption and biosorption for pollutant removal

papers.abstract: Abstract Sustainable asphalt technologies are increasingly vital for conserving resources, reducing environmental emissions, and enabling the beneficial reuse of carbon-rich waste materials. Surface-functionalized biochar (SFB) offers a promising strategy to enhance asphalt performance, while providing a sustainable platform for mitigating volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions; however, the roles of environmental humidity and asphalt binder composition in governing SFB’s VOC-mitigation efficacy remain poorly understood. Here, we evaluate SFB-modified asphalt at relative humidity (RH) ≈ 50% and 50 °C using environmental chamber measurements, volatility- and polarity-resolved emission analysis, molecular dynamics simulations, and density functional theory calculations. Across three asphalt binders, SFB reduced total organic emission factors by 94.5%, 84.5%, and 46.7%. Intermediate-volatility organic compounds (IVOCs) and semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs) were consistently suppressed by more than 70%, but light-polar VOC emissions showed an increase specifically in one out of the three binders. This in turn demonstrates that mitigation under humid conditions is strongly binder-dependent. Simulations indicate that interfacial water redistributes polar VOCs and competes with them for adsorption sites, weakening SFB–VOC interactions, particularly for small polar compounds. Unlike earlier studies focused mainly on dry-condition mitigation, the present work links binder-dependent humid-condition measurements with molecular-level competitive adsorption mechanisms. Study outcomes highlight the need to design emission-mitigation strategies tailored to specific climatic regions, where material chemistry and humidity conditions can govern suppressant effectiveness in real-world environments.

papers.title: Probing Adsorbed Water in Al(HCOO)3 Metal–Organic Framework by Multinuclear and Multidimensional Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Water affects the local structure, dynamics, and adsorption properties of metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), yet the molecular-level characterization of confined water remains difficult due to the lack of long-range ordering. Here, we study the water adsorption in microporous MOF Al(HCOO)3 using multinuclear solid-state NMR spectroscopy combined with ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. 1H NMR resolves two distinct confined-water environments and reveals water–framework and water–water contacts. 13C and 27Al NMR further show that water adsorption perturbs the local environments of the formate linkers and AlO6 coordination units. Powder X-ray diffraction shows that the long-range crystalline framework is preserved after water loading, whereas 13C NMR detects a minor mobile formate-containing species that disappears upon re-dehydration, consistent with the partial local hydrolysis of the framework. 2H NMR distinguishes both highly mobile and confined water undergoing rapid anisotropic reorientation. The effective quadrupolar line shape is consistent with rapid anisotropic reorientation, for which C2-axis flips provide one possible motional model. 1H–2H CP-HETCOR NMR further suggests dipolar contacts between restricted water molecules, the formate framework, and neighboring water molecules. AIMD simulations support water–framework interactions associated with the two pore environments and the formation of an interconnected water network. These results provide molecular-level insights into the water adsorption sites and dynamics in Al(HCOO)3 and the previously unreported partial hydrolysis of this MOF.

papers.abstract: Abstract The electrostatic properties of the Au(111)/self-assembled monolayer (SAM)/electrolyte interface were investigated using density functional theory combined with the effective screening medium and reference interaction site model (DFT-ESM-RISM) with explicit counterions. The resulting interfacial structure can be described as a quasi-two-dimensional carboxylate–counterion ionic crystal. The calculated potential of zero charge (PZC) shifts exhibit weak dependence on bulk electrolyte concentration and are consistent with available experimental data for Na+ systems. To clarify the microscopic origin of the PZC shifts, the electrostatic potential profiles were decomposed into contributions arising from the SAM dipole, the carboxylate–counterion ionic layer, and polarized interfacial water. The analysis reveals that the water contribution dominates for Na+, whereas the ionic contribution becomes increasingly important for K+ and Cs+. The results indicate that the electrostatic response of the interface is governed primarily by local counterion–carboxylate organization within the SAM termination region and the resulting polarization of interfacial water. These findings provide a molecular-level explanation of experimentally observed PZC shifts and establish the electrostatic consequences of local counterion–carboxylate organization and the resulting polarization of interfacial water.

papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Electrochemical CO 2 reduction toward multicarbon (C 2+ ) products remains challenging because conventional Cu catalysts lack the ability to simultaneously optimize intermediate stabilization, proton transfer, and C─C coupling kinetics. Here we report a high‐voltage electrospinning‐assisted defect engineering strategy to regulate the electronic structure of Cu catalysts for selective C 2+ electrosynthesis. Defect‐rich CuO nanowire precursors were fabricated by high‐voltage electrospinning and subsequently reconstructed into oxide‐derived Cu (OD‐Cu) nanowires enriched with abundant electronically perturbed Cu sites. The resulting OD‐Cu nanowires exhibit substantially enhanced C 2+ selectivity compared with conventional Cu catalysts. Mechanistic studies reveal that high‐voltage electrospinning‐assisted defects reorganize the reorganization of the interfacial water configuration and proton‐transfer dynamics while strengthening Cu─ * CO π‐backbonding interactions, thereby optimizing * CO stabilization and promoting hydrogen‐assisted C─C coupling. This work establishes a direct correlation between high‐voltage electrospinning‐assisted defect regulation, electronic structure modulation and multicarbon formation kinetics, providing a general strategy for designing efficient Cu catalysts for selective C 2+ electrosynthesis.

papers.abstract: The self-propelled catamaran towing method, which enables a 5kn transportation speed of the immersed tunnel, has been successfully pioneered in Shenzhen-Zhongshan Link. Nevertheless, the deep draft and low freeboard of the tunnel element render long-distance towing highly susceptible to prominent shallow water effect and bank restriction, which have not been systematically investigated in previous studies. To address this research gap, comprehensive towing tank experiments under diverse channel conditions are performed to explore the influences of confined water environments on the resistance and propulsion performance of the coupled catamaran-tunnel system. The results indicate that the tunnel segment remarkably amplifies confined water interference during transportation, with the total resistance and resistance coefficient of the integrated towing system reaching 14.20 times and 6.73 times those of the independent catamaran, respectively. The superposition of shallow-water and bank effects further increases the system resistance by 58.4% and raises the required delivered power by 83.7%. Furthermore, empirical formulas correlating resistance and propulsion efficiency with depth-to-draft ratio and Froude number are derived, which offer dependable references for engineering practice.

papers.title: Forward Waveform Transfer of Rotational Cliff Collapse-Induced Waves for Early Warning Assessment of Wave Hazards in Water Bodies
papers.abstract: Rotational collapse of a cliff into a confined water body can generate a high-energy leading wave group that reaches exposed shores within a short time. Improved hazard assessment therefore requires a practical link between an earlier near-source water level observation and the evolving downstream wave response. This study quantifies that link by reconstructing the downstream leading wave group generated by rotational cliff collapse from an earlier upstream waveform. Paired gauge records from 79 physical experiments were analyzed over a 0.50 m propagation interval. A forward waveform transfer model was evaluated using nested source-configuration-grouped validation, with the downstream evaluation window defined independently of the measured downstream response. The median aligned waveform correlation was 0.989, while the median apparent celerity ratio, amplitude gain, and time-integrated squared wave elevation transmission ratio were 0.867, 0.578, and 0.412, respectively. Out-of-fold R2 values reached 0.840 for downstream waveform reconstruction and 0.915 for peak amplitude prediction, with positive performance across intact and fragmented source states. These findings establish a time-ordered hydrodynamic relation between near-source and downstream wave conditions, providing a basis for faster interpretation of developing cliff-collapse wave hazards and strengthening early warning assessment in reservoirs, lakes, fjords, and confined coastal inlets.

papers.abstract: This study presents a novel hydro-mechanical framework for assessing damage development in the toe zone of gentle piedmont slopes by integrating seepage analysis and beam theory. SEEP3D numerical simulations are performed to characterise pore-water pressure and confined water distributions under variable slope geometries, dimensions of water-blocking structures, and rainfall characteristics. Based on confined water distribution, the slope toe region is classified into two distinct zones. Zone A, featuring a triangular uplift pressure distribution, is analysed using a simply supported beam model, whereas Zone B, with a trapezoidal uplift pressure distribution, is idealised as a cantilever beam. The results reveal that slope length and the embedded depth of water-blocking structures exert the most significant control over seepage characteristics. Rainfall duration and intensity also govern confined water distribution, with V-shaped and incremental rainfall patterns exerting the most prominent impacts on seepage fields. Deformation and cracking behaviours within both zones are systematically investigated to quantify damage extent at the slope toe. The combined numerical simulation and mechanical modelling approach established herein provides a quantitative and mechanistic tool for evaluating slope stability and supporting landslide mitigation in gentle piedmont areas.

papers.abstract: Hydrogel electrolytes have emerged as promising platforms for stabilizing aqueous zinc‐ion batteries beyond their conventional roles as mechanically confined quasisolid electrolytes. Recent studies increasingly demonstrate that hydrogel‐confined electrochemical environments can dynamically regulate Zn 2+ solvation structures, ion‐transport behavior, hydrogen‐bond networks, and interfacial reaction pathways during electrochemical cycling. Such regulation mechanisms substantially influence concentration polarization, Zn nucleation behavior, desolvation kinetics, interfacial side reactions, and Zn deposition stability under repeated plating/stripping conditions. This review comprehensively discusses recent advances in hydrogel electrolytes for aqueous Zn‐ion batteries from the perspective of dynamic ion regulation and interfacial electrochemical stabilization. Particular emphasis is placed on confined water chemistry, polymer‐ion coordination, ion‐flux homogenization, interphase engineering, and electro‐chemo‐mechanical stabilization of dynamically evolving Zn interfaces. In addition, emerging hydrogel architectures together with advanced operando characterization approaches are highlighted to provide future perspectives for developing next‐generation hydrogel electrolytes capable of sustaining highly reversible and durable aqueous Zn electrochemistry.

papers.title: Water Inside the Carbon Cage—H2O@C60 and Related Fullerene Structures: Synthesis, Experimental Characterization, Computational Insights, and Future Perspectives
papers.abstract: The encapsulation of a single water molecule inside C60 has established H2O@C60 as a benchmark system for investigating molecular behavior under precisely defined subnanometer confinement. This review integrates advances in the synthesis, experimental characterization, theoretical description, and emerging applications of H2O@C60 and selected related water-containing fullerenes. Particular attention is given to molecular-surgery strategies, in which the fullerene cage is opened, loaded with water, and subsequently reconstructed, as well as to improvements that have increased encapsulation and cage-closure efficiencies and enabled isotopically labeled and heterofullerene derivatives. Structural, nuclear magnetic resonance, infrared, terahertz, neutron-scattering, dielectric, photoelectron, and single-molecule transport studies collectively show that the C60 framework remains highly rigid, while the confined water molecule retains pronounced translational, rotational, vibrational, and nuclear-spin dynamics. At the same time, weak but measurable host–guest interactions produce symmetry breaking, rotational-level splitting, electrostatic screening, modified vibrational responses, and environment-dependent ortho–para conversion. Computational studies, ranging from density functional and correlated wave-function methods to multidimensional quantum-dynamical and molecular-dynamics approaches, have been essential for interpreting these observations and defining the underlying potential-energy landscape. Related systems, including H2O@C70, H2O@C59N, charged azafullerenes, and isotopically substituted endofullerenes, provide routes to tune cage geometry and electrostatic interactions. Although technological applications remain largely at the proof-of-principle stage, these systems offer promising platforms for quantum spectroscopy, molecular electronics, and the rational design of functional host–guest nanomaterials.

papers.title: From Accurate Quantum Chemistry to Converged Thermodynamics for Ion Pairing in Solution
papers.source: Journal of the American Chemical Society

authors.name: Niamh O'Neill
institutions: Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research

papers.abstract: Abstract Quantitative prediction of thermodynamic properties in solution is essential for translating atomistic simulations into reliable chemical insight. As an exemplar system, the behavior of CaCO3 in water has been widely studied to understand its mineralization in seawater, with potential implications for carbon-capture strategies. However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO3 with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the “gold-standard” coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO3 ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.

papers.abstract: We assess the non-linear version of the Entropy Stable Extension to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations which were originally derived in arXiv:2407.17334. Using an identity for the derivative of the inverse of linearized collision operator, we show that the Entropy Stable Extension takes the form of a fourth-order quasi-cubic system of equations when written in entropy variables. Furthermore, we find that the quasi-linear contributions to the extension retain the highest order derivative contributions and the entropy stability of the full extension. This quasi-linear approximation is applied to the stationary heat transfer between parallel plates where we find that a specification of the boundary conditions that interpolates between the continuum and collisions limits can yield temperature profiles that better agree with DSMC predictions than Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with Smoluchowski boundary conditions, while also giving a heat flux prediction that better agrees with the Sherman-Lees heat flux than the Navier-Stokes-Fourier prediction. We conclude with a brief study of dispersion of plane waves according to the linearized equations in one dimension where we show that all frequency modes are stable and relate this to entropy stability.

papers.title: Coordination Bridges in Confined‐Water Domains Enable Partially Desolvated Zn 2 + Transport in Aqueous Zinc‐Ion Batteries
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Zinc‐ion batteries (ZIBs), owing to their intrinsic safety and cost competitiveness, are attracting significant interest as next‐generation energy storage system (ESS) technologies. However, their commercialization is severely hindered by poor cycle stability, primarily originating from dendritic Zn growth and parasitic hydrogen evolution. To address these challenges simultaneously, we design and integrate a multifunctional polymeric protective layer incorporating amide and imidazolium functional groups. The zincophilic amide groups facilitate ion transport by providing stable Zn 2+ binding sites, whereas the hygroscopic imidazolium groups establish a confined‐water domain that regulates local solvation dynamics. Within this domain, water molecules transiently stabilize Zn 2+ and act as a coordination bridge during ion migration, yet their mobility toward the electrode surface is restricted. This dual functionality increases the Zn 2+ single‐ion conductivity 6.55‐fold and reduces the hydrogen evolution rate by 79.1%. Consequently, Zn//Zn symmetric cells exhibit markedly extended cycling lifetimes of up to 2200 h at 1 mA cm −2 and 1 mAh cm −2 . When applied to Zn–I 2 full cells, the protective layer enables stable operation over 4000 cycles with >85% capacity retention, even under a practical areal capacity of 3.6 mAh cm −2 . These findings highlight a robust interfacial strategy to realize long‐duration, high‐capacity aqueous ZIBs for grid‐scale energy storage.

papers.title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
papers.abstract: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.

papers.title: Fully coupled two-dimensional numerical simulation of wave interaction with an elastic wall in a narrow gap
papers.abstract: Narrow-gap resonance is commonly investigated under rigid-wall assumptions, although deformable boundaries occur in many confined-water systems. This study aims to clarify how elastic-wall deformation and the geometry of the bottom passage affect the coupled hydrodynamic and structural responses of an open-top confined-water system. A two-dimensional strongly coupled partitioned finite volume method–finite element method model, implemented using OpenFOAM, CalculiX, and preCICE, is validated against published hydroelastic results and wave-flume measurements. Wall stiffness and draft are varied to evaluate the local flow, confined free-surface motion, wave reflection and dissipation, hydrodynamic loading, wall displacement, and response phase. The results show that decreasing wall stiffness increases wall deformation and weakens the high-velocity region beneath the wall, thereby reducing the free-surface oscillation inside the confined region. The near-rigid and moderately elastic cases retain a low-reflection–high-dissipation response within a similar frequency range, whereas the most flexible case weakens this feature, with a higher reflection minimum and a lower dissipation maximum. The most flexible wall exhibits reduced load amplitudes at intermediate and higher frequencies, together with a more pronounced phase lag. Reducing the wall draft enlarges the bottom passage, shifts the reflection minimum and dissipation maximum toward higher frequencies, and decreases both load and displacement amplitudes. The results provide guidance for selecting wall stiffness and draft in flexible wave-energy devices and elastic coastal-protection components.

papers.abstract: A deep foundation pit of Wuhan Metro Line 12 is located in the water-rich sand layer on the first terrace of the Yangtze River. Under the influence of foundation pit dewatering, the vertical surface deformation increases significantly after excavation enters the confined water-rich fine sand layer. The lateral deformation of the diaphragm wall increases with increasing excavation depth, and the wall deformation curve shows an “arch” profile. The maximum horizontal displacement gradually moves downward as the excavation depth increases. After excavation reaches the confined water-rich fine sand layer, the wall deformation increases significantly, with a maximum increase of 161%. The lateral water and earth pressure in the standard section of the supporting structure of the foundation pit is mainly borne by the second steel pipe brace, while that at the pit corners is mainly borne by the third and fourth reinforced concrete braces.
